title: Privacy, Confidentiality, and Security

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish among privacy, confidentiality, and security and explain how they relate to one another.
- Classify safeguards as administrative, physical, or technical and give examples of each.
- Apply safeguards to protect PHI in paper, oral, and electronic forms.
- Recognize and escalate privacy or security concerns, including suspected breaches, to the appropriate person.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Privacy is like owning a diary: you get to decide who is allowed to read it.

### Question 2

Confidentiality is like being trusted with a secret and promising to keep it safe.

### Question 3

Security is like the locks, alarms, and secret codes that keep something valuable safe.

### Question 4

Privacy is the "what" (your right), confidentiality is the "promise" (to keep it), and security is the "how" (the locks and codes).

### Question 5

Confidentiality is the act of keeping a secret; security is the lock on the box.

### Question 6

Privacy is your say-so over who may look at your private information.

### Question 7

A password is like a key to a locker; security is the key itself.

### Question 8

Move the screen so only the right person can see it, like turning your test paper away from a classmate.

### Question 9

Administrative safeguards are the rules and lessons that tell people what to do.

### Question 10

A lock on a cabinet is like a lock on your front door—it keeps things safe in the real world.

### Question 11

Encryption is like writing a message in a secret code that only the right person can read.

### Question 12

A badge to open a door is like a special key that only certain people have.

### Question 13

The rule "never share keys" is a rule (administrative); the key itself is a tool (technical).

### Question 14

A risk analysis is like checking all the windows and doors of your house to find the weak spots.

### Question 15

A business associate agreement is like a written promise from a helper that they will keep secrets too.

### Question 16

These rules decide who is allowed to work with private information and what happens if someone breaks the rules.

### Question 17

Turn the screen away, like you turn your notebook away from a neighbor.

### Question 18

Shredding is like tearing up a secret note into tiny pieces so no one can put it back together.

### Question 19

A badge is like a house key—only people who should be inside get one.

### Question 20

Lock the laptop in a safe AND put a secret code on it—two layers of protection.

### Question 21

Grab the private paper as soon as it arrives so no one else can read it.

### Question 22

Your own username and secret password are like your own key to the computer.

### Question 23

Automatic logoff is like a door that locks itself if you forget.

### Question 24

An audit log is like a visitor book that writes down everyone who came in and when.

### Question 25

Sending through a secure channel is like mailing a letter in a locked box instead of on a postcard.

### Question 26

It is like needing both a key AND a secret code to open the door.

### Question 27

Updates and antivirus are like a shield and a flu shot for the computer.

### Question 28

Don't open a strange letter promising a prize—show it to a trusted adult first.

### Question 29

Call someone by their first name quietly, not their full name and secret reason.

### Question 30

Don't talk about secrets in the hallway—wait until you're in a private room.

### Question 31

Before telling a secret to someone, make sure they are really allowed to know it.

### Question 32

If you see someone peeking at a secret they should not, tell a trusted adult.

### Question 33

Only take the smallest slice you need, not the whole pie.

### Question 34

Fill in only the boxes the form asks for—don't add extra secrets.

### Question 35

Double-check the address before mailing a secret letter.

### Question 36

You have the right to see your own notebook—it is about you.

### Question 37

The notice is like a rulebook that tells patients how their secrets will be handled.

### Question 38

Sharing beyond normal care needs the patient's written "yes."

### Question 39

You can't sell your friends' secrets to a company without their permission.

### Question 40

If two rules protect a secret, follow the one that protects it more.

### Question 41

If someone asks a private question in a crowd, move to a quiet corner to answer.

### Question 42

Put secret papers back in the locked drawer before you go home.

### Question 43

When you print a secret, go get it right away.

### Question 44

Keep secret stuff on a safe, locked device and don't leave it lying around.

### Question 45

Never put someone else's private information or picture online without permission.

### Question 46

Even "when is the appointment" is a secret—check first.

### Question 47

If something goes wrong, tell the person in charge right away so they can fix it.

### Question 48

A breach is when a secret gets out when it should not have.

### Question 49

De-identification is like erasing the name tag so you can't tell whose it is.

### Question 50

Keep the list of who is visiting private, like a secret guest list.

### Question 51

The Security Rule is the "how to keep computer secrets safe" rule.

### Question 52

The Privacy Rule is the "who can see your health secrets" rule.

### Question 53

Locks and codes (security) make it possible to keep your promise (privacy and confidentiality).

### Question 54

Don't leave the key to the safe sitting on top of the safe.

### Question 55

Lock your desk before you go to lunch, just like locking your bike.

### Question 56

Secrets can be written, spoken, or typed—all three need protecting.

### Question 57

Whisper secrets, don't shout them.

### Question 58

When leaving a message, just say "please call back," not all the secrets.

### Question 59

To keep a treasure safe you need a rule, a lock, AND a code—all three together.

### Question 60

Make sure the address is right and use a locked envelope before sending secrets.

### Question 61

An incidental disclosure is like a name being briefly heard when someone walks by—unavoidable even when you are careful.

### Question 62

Erase all your secrets off a device before giving it away.

### Question 63

Contingency planning is like having a spare key and a flashlight ready for an emergency.

### Question 64

Even when the lights go out, keep secrets safe.

### Question 65

Check someone is really who they say before telling them secrets.

### Question 66

Each person gets a key only to the drawers they need.

### Question 67

Never lend your key to someone else, even for a minute.

### Question 68

Make sure it is the right person before telling them the plan.

### Question 69

Protect secrets no matter if they are typed, spoken, or written.

### Question 70

Only tell secrets to people who truly need to know to help.

### Question 71

Turn the paper over so no one can read it.

### Question 72

A privacy filter is like tinted glasses that hide your screen from people nearby.

### Question 73

Even without a name, enough clues can tell people who it is.

### Question 74

Carry the private papers yourself; don't leave them lying around.

### Question 75

If something valuable and secret is stolen, tell the person in charge right away.

### Question 76

When unsure whether to tell a secret, ask the person in charge first.

### Question 77

Put the secret in a sealed envelope with the right address.

### Question 78

Don't let visitors use the machine that sends secrets.

### Question 79

Check who they are quietly, like showing an ID at a private counter.

### Question 80

A rule written down telling people what to do is a "rules" safeguard.

### Question 81

When a serious official letter arrives, give it to the person in charge.

### Question 82

The privacy officer is like the "safety captain" for secrets.

### Question 83

The best safety comes from using many layers: rules, locks, AND codes.

### Question 84

Take the letter straight to the person it is for without reading it.

### Question 85

If someone asks you to call their cell instead of home, do what they ask.
